question: Which of these best describes an algorithm?
correct: A finite list of unambiguous steps that solves a problem
incorrect: Any program, as long as it compiles and runs without errors
A routine for searching or sorting, the two jobs algorithms do
A diagram of boxes and arrows showing how a program flows
feedback: An algorithm is the plan, not the program: a limited number of steps, each clear enough that nobody has to guess what it means. A program is one way of writing an algorithm down and a flowchart is one way of drawing it, but a recipe or a set of directions can be an algorithm too. Searching and sorting are famous examples, not the definition.

question: Which of these are properties an algorithm must have?
correct: Definiteness: each step is precise, with no room for interpretation
Finiteness: it stops after a limited number of steps
Effectiveness: each step is basic enough to actually carry out
Input and output: it takes defined inputs and produces a result
incorrect: Efficiency: it uses the fewest steps possible for the problem
Language: it is written in a programming language such as Java
feedback: Definite, finite, effective, with inputs and an output: those four make something an algorithm. Efficiency is what makes one algorithm better than another, not what makes it an algorithm; a slow linear search is still an algorithm. And an algorithm exists before any code does: it can be written in pseudocode, drawn as a flowchart, or spoken aloud.

question: “Give the goldfish some food whenever it looks hungry.” Why does this fail as an algorithm?
correct: Its steps are vague: “some food” and “looks hungry” are not precise
incorrect: It has no input: nothing is handed to it before it begins
It never ends: a goldfish has to be fed again every day
It is not written in Java or any other programming language
feedback: An algorithm's steps have to be precise enough that nobody has to guess. How much is “some”? What does hungry look like? Compare: “At 9:00 and 18:00, drop exactly 3 pellets into the tank.” An algorithm may take no input at all, and it does not have to be written in a programming language.

question: A loop and an if together make an algorithm. What does this one print?
feedback: The loop visits every element, and the if lets only the matching ones add to the count: index 0 and index 2. Text is compared with .equals(). Starting at 0 and adding 1 for each match is the counting pattern you will meet again below.

question: Match each flowchart symbol to what it stands for.

pairs.definition: The start or the end of the whole process
An action or calculation, such as total = total + 1
A yes/no question with two paths leading out

feedback: Ovals mark where the process starts and ends, rectangles do the work, parallelograms move data in or out, and arrows give the order. The diamond is the only shape with two ways out, which is why every if and every loop test in a flowchart is drawn as one.

question: In a flowchart, a diamond asks  n > 0?  Its Yes arrow leads to a rectangle holding  n = n - 1, and an arrow from that rectangle leads back up to the diamond. Its No arrow leads on to End. Which Java construct does this shape describe?
incorrect: An if statement
An if-else statement
A switch statement
feedback: An arrow that travels back to an earlier diamond is what makes a loop; an if, an if-else or a switch only ever flows forward. The question is asked before the rectangle runs, so the body might run zero times — exactly how a while loop behaves.

question:
Trace this pseudocode. What number does it display?
SET total TO 0
SET n TO {{a}}
WHILE n > 0
    ADD n TO total
    SUBTRACT {{s}} FROM n
END WHILE
DISPLAY total
feedback_template: n starts at {{a}} and drops by {{s}} on every pass. Each value of n that is still above 0 is added to total, and those values add up to {{expected}}. The test sits at the top of the loop, so once n reaches 0 or less nothing more is added. Keeping a two-column table (n, total) is the reliable way to trace it.

question: Arrange this pseudocode, first step to last, so that it displays the average of a list of scores.
items: FOR EACH score IN scores: ADD score TO total
SET average TO total / NUMBER OF scores
feedback: Each step needs the one before it: total must exist before anything is added to it, the division is only meaningful once every score is in, and there is nothing to display until average has been computed. Pseudocode lets you settle that order before worrying about Java's syntax.

question: Arrange the steps of a linear search for a target value, first to last.
items: Start at the first element, index 0
Compare the current element with the target
If they match, report the index and stop
Otherwise, move on to the next element
If the elements run out, report “not found”
feedback: Linear search checks the elements one by one from the front. A match ends it at once; otherwise it moves along and compares again. Only when every element has been checked can it say the target is not there — so an algorithm for searching has to handle both endings.

question: The Java keyword that ends a loop immediately, abandoning any passes that were still to come, is ___.
feedback: break jumps straight out of the nearest enclosing loop, and execution carries on with the first statement after it. It is the same keyword that ends a case in a switch. Compare continue, which gives up only the current pass and keeps looping.

feedback_template: The break is tested before sum += i on each pass, so when i reaches {{k}} the loop ends without adding {{k}}. Only the values below {{k}} were added, giving {{expected}}. The header says i <= 10, but break overrides it.

question: The search code written in this course reports the index where the target was found. Why does it report -1, rather than 0, when the target is absent?
correct: 0 is a real index, so it would look like a match at the front
incorrect: -1 is what Java stores in an int that was never assigned
0 would stop the loop before the last element is checked
-1 is the index just past the end of any array
feedback: The answer is an index, and every index from 0 to length - 1 means “found here”, so “not found” needs a value that can never be an index. -1 is the usual choice. It is a convention, not something Java supplies: the code has to set it, usually by starting the variable at -1 before the loop.

question: A linear search checks an array of {{n}} elements from index 0 upward and stops as soon as it meets the target, which is sitting at index {{k}}. How many elements did it compare with the target?
feedback_template: Indexes start at 0, so reaching index {{k}} means indexes 0 through {{k}} were all compared: {{expected}} elements. The rest of the {{n}} are never looked at, which is what stopping early buys. Had the target been absent, all {{n}} would have been compared.

question: The target appears more than once in this array. What does the search print?
feedback: Nothing stops this loop once it has a match, so it keeps going and idx is overwritten at index 0, again at index 2, and finally at index 4. It reports the LAST match. Adding break; after idx = i; would leave the loop at the first match and print 0, and would save the wasted comparisons as well.

prompt: Complete this search so that found ends up true only if the target is in the array, and the loop stops as soon as it is seen.
feedback: A boolean flag starts at false — nothing has been found yet — and is switched to true at the moment of a match. break then leaves the loop, because there is no point checking the rest. After the loop, found tells you which way it went.

question: An accumulator is a variable that builds up a result as a loop runs. Match each kind to how it starts and what it does on each pass.

pairs.definition: Starts at 0 and adds each value on
Starts at 0 and adds 1 when a test passes
Starts at 1 and multiplies by each value
Starts at the first element and keeps the larger
Starts at "" and joins each piece on

feedback: Every accumulator is set up before the loop, updated inside it and used after it. The starting value is the one that changes nothing: 0 for adding, 1 for multiplying, "" for joining. A maximum is the exception — it has to start from a real element, because any number you make up might be larger than everything in the array.

feedback_template: total holds {{s}} before the loop, and each pass adds one element to it, so it ends at {{expected}}. Whatever the accumulator holds before the loop is part of the answer. That is why a sum is normally started at 0, the one value that adds nothing.

prompt: Fill in the starting values and the counter's update so that all three results come out right.
feedback: Start every accumulator at the value that changes nothing: 1 for a product (starting at 0 would make every product 0), 0 for a counter, false for a flag that flips to true when the target is seen. A counter goes up by exactly one for each element that passes the test, whatever that element's value is.

question: Which statements about accumulator loops are correct?
correct: Writing  total = 0;  inside the loop body wipes the running total on every pass
One loop can keep a sum and a counter going at the same time
incorrect: An accumulator declared inside the loop body can still be printed after the loop
A local int that is given no starting value begins at 0 on its own
The update  total = v;  does the same job as  total += v;
feedback: The accumulator has to be declared and given its starting value before the loop. Reset it inside and only the last element survives; declare it inside and it no longer exists after the closing brace (the compiler reports it cannot find the symbol). Java also refuses to read a local variable that was never assigned, rather than quietly using 0. And  total = v  replaces the total where  total += v  adds to it. One pass over the data can feed as many accumulators as you like, which is how an average gets its sum and its count.

question: An accumulator can build text as well as a number. What does this program print?
feedback: all starts as the empty String, and each pass joins the next name onto the end of it: "Al", then "AlBo", then "AlBoCy". Nothing is put between the names, because nothing in the code asks for a space.

question: NPC: The maximum that was never in the array
intro: Nia unrolls a miner's log of depth readings, every one below zero. “Find me the largest reading,” she says. “I will do it the way most apprentices do first.”

steps.say: max is just a variable that remembers the largest element met so far. I start it at 0 and let every element challenge it.

beats.say: max is just a variable that remembers the largest element met so far. I started it at 0, and each element challenges it in turn.

steps.say: Trace it. Is -4 greater than 0? No. Is -9? No. Is -2? No. The if never succeeds.

check.prompt: So what does the program print?
check.why: No element ever beat 0, so max was never updated. It prints 0, a number that is not even in the array.

steps.say: The repair: start max from a real element, the first one. Then -9 fails to beat -4, -2 does beat it, and the answer is -2.

beats.say: The starting value was the bug: 0 was my invention, not a reading. The repair is to start from a real element, the first one.
Now max begins at -4. -9 fails to beat it, -2 does beat it, and the program prints -2. The same rule holds for a minimum: start from an element of the array, never from a number you made up.

outro: “The next monster made the same mistake while hunting for a minimum. Trace what its code really prints.”

question: This code is meant to find the lowest temperature. Trace it: what does it actually print?
feedback: 12, 7 and 9 are all larger than 0, so the if never succeeds and min keeps its made-up starting value. The output, 0, is not even an element of the array. Starting with  int min = temps[0];  fixes it: then 7 replaces 12, 9 fails to replace 7, and the code prints 7.

question: A loop is finding the largest value in an int array a, remembering it in a variable named max. The test  if (a[i] > max)  has just come out true. Write the one statement that belongs inside that if.
feedback: When the current element beats the best so far, it becomes the new best: max = a[i];  The assignment copies right to left, so writing a[i] = max; would overwrite the array with the old maximum instead of remembering the new one.

incorrect: sum / count
(double) (sum / count)
sum / count + 0.0
feedback: sum / count divides one int by another, which throws away the fraction and gives 8. The cast (double) sum turns sum into 41.0 before the division, so the fraction is kept. Casting the finished result, or adding 0.0 to it, is too late: the .2 has already gone.

question: Inside a loop body, what does the statement continue; do?
correct: It skips the rest of this pass and moves on to the next pass of the loop
incorrect: It leaves the loop at once and carries on with the code after the loop
It does nothing on its own: it marks where the loop resumes after a pause
It restarts the whole loop from the beginning, with the counter reset too
feedback: continue abandons the current pass only. In a for loop the update (such as i++) still runs, the condition is tested again, and the loop carries on if it is true. Leaving the loop altogether is a different statement. Nothing in Java resets a loop counter for you.

feedback_template: continue abandons the rest of the body for that one pass only: i++ still runs and the loop carries on. So the multiples of {{k}} between 1 and {{n}} are skipped, and the other {{expected}} values of i reach count++. This is a counter with a filter in front of it.

question: This loop skips some of its passes. What does the program print?
feedback: continue abandons the rest of the current pass and moves on to the next one. For -2 the if is true, so total += e[i] is skipped for that element only. 5 and 7 are added as usual, giving 12. Unlike break, continue does not end the loop.

break ends the whole loop, so everything from that pass onward is lost: breaking at 3 leaves 12, and breaking on the very first pass (1 < 3) leaves nothing. continue skips only the print of the current pass: skipping 3 alone gives 1245, skipping everything above 3 gives 123, and skipping everything below 3 gives 345.

question: NPC: One value, many doors
intro: Nia stands where the corridor splits into a row of numbered doors. “When ONE value decides which of many doors you take, a long chain of else-ifs gets tiresome. Java has a tool made for the job.”

steps.say: Java works out the value in the round brackets once, then jumps to the case that matches it. default is the door for “none of the above”, like a final else.

beats.say: This is a switch. Java works out the value in the round brackets once, then jumps to the case that matches it.
default is the door for “none of the above”, like the final else of a chain.

check.why: Java jumps straight to case 2, prints cheese, and the break then takes it out of the switch.

steps.say: A case label only says where to START. Without a break, Java keeps going straight into the next case. That is called fall-through.

beats.say: Each case ends with break, which leaves the switch. That matters more than it looks, because a case label only says where to START.
Here the first break is missing. Without it, Java keeps going straight into the next case. That is called fall-through, and forgetting a break is the classic switch bug.

check.prompt: coins is 1, and the first break is missing. What is printed?
check.why: Java enters at case 1 and prints bread. Nothing stops it there, so it carries on into case 2 and prints cheese before the break ends the switch.

steps.say: Now and then fall-through is what you want: two labels stacked together share the same code.

beats.say: Now and then fall-through is exactly what you want. Two labels stacked together share the same code.

outro: “Find the matching case, then run until a break. The next monsters leave some breaks out on purpose.”

question: A switch can choose on a String as well as on a number. What does this program print?
feedback: dept holds "HEALTH", so Java jumps to that case and prints Floor 4. The break then leaves the switch, so default is never reached. default runs only when no case matches at all.

question: Two case labels are stacked together here. What does this program print?
feedback: case 6 has no code of its own, so entering there would fall straight through to case 7. That is how two values share one block: 6 and 7 both print Rest. The break stops the fall-through before it reaches default.

question: This switch is missing some of its break statements. What is printed?
feedback: In a switch, case labels are only entry points. Java jumps to case 2, prints B, and then falls through into case 3 because nothing stopped it, printing C. The break after C finally leaves the switch, so D is not printed. A is skipped because execution entered below it. Fall-through is the classic bug of a switch: every case that should stop needs a break of its own.

prompt: Fill in the three keywords this switch is missing.
feedback: case introduces each value to match. break leaves the switch at the end of a case; without it, 5 stars would print Outstanding and then Good as well. default catches every value that no case names, the way a final else does.

question: A linear search looks for a target in an array of n elements. Match each case to what it costs.

pairs.definition: 1 comparison: the target is the first element
n comparisons: the target is last, or missing
About n / 2 comparisons: it is somewhere in the middle

feedback: How long a search takes depends on where the target is. If it is first, one comparison is enough. If it is last, or not there at all, every element has to be compared. On average the search gets about halfway before it finds what it wants.

question: An array holds {{n}} elements, and the target is not among them. How many elements does a linear search compare with the target before it can report “not found”?
feedback_template: A linear search can only say “not found” after it has looked at everything, so all {{expected}} elements are compared. This is its worst case — the same cost as finding the target in the very last position.

question: In the worst case a linear search compares the target with every element, so doubling the size of the array doubles the work. In Big-O notation, linear search is described as O(___).
feedback: O(n), read “order n”: the work grows in step with n, the number of elements. Ten elements, up to ten comparisons; a million elements, up to a million. Big-O describes how the worst case scales as the input grows, not how long any one run takes.

question: Why do programmers usually judge an algorithm by its worst case?
correct: It is a guarantee: the algorithm will never do worse than that
incorrect: It is the case that turns up most often with real-world data
It is the only one of the three cases that can be measured
It is always about twice the cost of the average case
feedback: The worst case is a promise about every input: however unlucky the data, the algorithm will not take longer than this. The best case tells you only what happens when you are lucky, and the average case depends on what “typical” input looks like, which is harder to pin down.

question: NPC: Three markers on a sorted shelf
intro: Seven numbered scrolls sit in order on a shelf. Nia sets three brass markers beside them, labelled low, mid and high. “Binary search is nothing more than moving these three,” she says.

steps.say: low and high fence in the part of the array where the target could still be. mid is the index halfway between them, and it is the only element I examine: one probe.

beats.say: I am hunting for 23 in a sorted array:
low and high fence in the indexes where the target could still be. mid is the index halfway between them, and nums[mid] is the only element I examine. That is one probe: nums[3] is 12.

steps.say: 12 is smaller than 23, and the array is sorted.

check.prompt: 12 is smaller than 23, and the array is sorted. Which indexes can still hold 23?
check.why: Everything left of index 3 is even smaller than 12, and index 3 itself has just been examined, so low jumps to mid + 1 = 4.

steps.say: Second probe: mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5, and nums[5] is 23. Found in two probes. Each probe halves what is left, so the worst case is: halve the size until 1 element remains, then add one probe for that last element. 7, 3, 1 is two halvings, so 3 probes at most.

beats.say: Second probe: low is 4 and high is 6, so mid is 5, and nums[5] is 23. Found, in two probes.

Each probe throws away half of what is left. To get the worst case, halve the size (dropping fractions) until 1 element remains, then add one probe for that last element. For 7 elements: 7, 3, 1 is two halvings, so 3 probes at most.

outro: “The next monster's search prints mid on every pass. Move the markers yourself and write down each mid.”

question: This binary search prints mid on every pass. What is its complete output?
feedback: Pass 1: low 0, high 8, mid 4; nums[4] is 21, too big, so high becomes 3. Pass 2: mid is (0 + 3) / 2 = 1 by int division; nums[1] is 6, too small, so low becomes 2. Pass 3: mid is (2 + 3) / 2 = 2; nums[2] is 10, found. Three probes for nine elements, where a linear search would also have needed three here but could need nine.

question:
Partway through a binary search, low is {{lo}} and high is {{hi}}. What value does this statement store?
int mid = (low + high) / 2;
feedback_template: low + high is {{total}}, and dividing one int by another drops any fraction, so mid is {{expected}}. When the sum is odd there is no exact middle, and the search simply probes the lower of the two middle indexes.

question: In a binary search loop that runs  while (low <= high), an apprentice writes  low = mid;  where the standard code has  low = mid + 1;  What is the risk?
correct: The range can stop shrinking, so the loop may never end
incorrect: The element at mid is skipped and can never be found
The search still works but needs about twice the probes
mid can pass high and index beyond the end of the array
feedback: Suppose low is 4 and high is 5. mid is (4 + 5) / 2 = 4, and if nums[4] is too small, low = mid sets low to 4 again: nothing changed, so the next pass is identical, forever. The + 1 is safe because index mid has just been examined and ruled out, and it guarantees the range shrinks on every pass. mid always lies between low and high, so it cannot run off the array.

question: This binary search is run on an array that is NOT in sorted order. The target 9 is in the array. What does it print?
feedback: The first probe is index 2, which holds 7. Since 7 < 9 the code throws away indexes 0 to 2, and the 9 at index 0 goes with them. The later probes (4, then 1) fail too, and idx stays -1. Binary search never looks at most of the array; it trusts the ordering to tell it where the target cannot be. On unsorted data that trust is misplaced, and it gives wrong answers without any error message.

question: The target is not in this sorted array. What does the search print?
feedback: Pass 1: mid is (0 + 7) / 2 = 3; 20 is too small, so low becomes 4. Pass 2: mid is (4 + 7) / 2 = 5; 31 is too big, so high becomes 4. Pass 3: mid is 4; 26 is too small, so low becomes 5. Now low (5) is greater than high (4): the fenced-in range is empty, the loop ends, and idx still holds -1. A miss is detected when low and high cross, after only 3 of the 8 elements were examined.

question: A sorted array holds {{n}} elements. In the worst case, how many elements does a standard binary search examine before it can stop?
feedback_template: Each probe discards at least half of what is left. {{n}} can be halved (dropping fractions) {{halvings}} times before only 1 element remains, and that last element still has to be examined: {{expected}} probes. Watch the exact powers of 2: 1,000 elements need 10 probes at most, but 1,024 need 11.

question: Each probe of a binary search halves what is left to search, so doubling the array adds just one probe. In Big-O notation, with n elements, its worst case is written O(___).
feedback: The number of times n can be halved before reaching 1 is its base-2 logarithm, so binary search is O(log n). Big-O ignores the base and any small constant, which is why log n, log₂ n and lg n all name the same growth rate. Compare linear search's O(n): at a million elements that is about 20 probes against a possible 1,000,000.

question: A binary search over a sorted String[] named a cannot use < to compare two Strings. Which test is true exactly when target comes before a[mid] in dictionary order?
incorrect: target.compareTo(a[mid]) == -1
target.equals(a[mid]) < 0
target.compareTo(a[mid]) == true
feedback: compareTo answers with an int: negative when the first String comes earlier in dictionary order, zero when they match, positive when it comes later. The negative number is not promised to be -1 ("pear".compareTo("plum") is -7), so always test < 0. equals gives back a boolean, which can only say same-or-different, never which comes first. The order is by character code, so every capital letter sorts ahead of every lowercase one: "Zebra" comes before "apple".

question: Which statements about linear search and binary search are correct?
correct: Linear search gives the right answer on an array in any order
Binary search of 1,000 sorted elements needs at most 10 probes
For one lookup in a small unsorted array, linear search is the sensible choice
incorrect: Linear search has to examine every element even after it has met the target
Sorting the array first lowers linear search's worst-case number of comparisons
feedback: Linear search assumes nothing about order, and it can stop the moment it finds the target. Its worst case is a target that is absent, which costs n comparisons whether or not the data is sorted. Binary search is far faster on big sorted arrays (1,000 halves down to 1 in 9 steps, plus one last probe), but sorting just to do a single lookup costs more than the linear search it replaces.

question: A shop's array of 100,000 item codes is unsorted, never changes, and will be searched thousands of times a day. Which plan does the least total work?
correct: Sort it once, then use binary search for every lookup after that
incorrect: Use linear search every time, since sorting costs more than it saves
Use binary search straight away, since it needs so few probes
Sort it before each lookup, then use binary search on the result
feedback: Binary search on unsorted data gives wrong answers, so it cannot simply be used straight away. Sorting is expensive, but here the cost is paid once and then shared by thousands of lookups of about 17 probes each, instead of up to 100,000 comparisons each. Sorting again before every lookup throws that saving away. If the array were only going to be searched once, plain linear search would win.

question: For an unsorted int array of n elements, which of these jobs take time that grows in proportion to n (linear time)?
correct: Linear search for a value that turns out to be absent
incorrect: Binary search, once the array has been sorted
Reading the last element, a[n - 1]
Reading the first element, a[0]
feedback: Summing, finding the maximum and an unsuccessful linear search each visit every element once: n steps, so linear. Binary search needs only about log₂ n probes, far fewer than n. And reading one element by its index takes the same single step whether the array has ten elements or ten million.

question: NPC: return, in the middle of a loop
intro: Nia chalks a search on the wall, this time wrapped in a method. “You know how to stop a loop early with break. Inside a method there is something stronger.”

steps.say: return ends the method on the spot, loop and all. So inside a method it does the job that break does elsewhere — and hands back the answer at the same time.

beats.say: These rounds work as before: I give the first line of a method, you write what goes between the braces, and Run costs nothing.
Look at return i. A return ends the method on the spot, loop and all. So inside a method it does the job that break does elsewhere, and hands back the answer at the same time.

check.prompt: nums is {4, 9, 4} and target is 4. What does the method hand back?
check.why: The first pass finds a match at index 0 and returns at once. The later 4, at index 2, is never looked at.

steps.say: The return after the loop is reached only when the loop has finished without finding anything. Put it inside the loop, in an else, and the method gives up after one element.

beats.say: The last line, return -1, is reached only when the loop has finished without finding anything.
Put it inside the loop instead — in an else — and the method gives up after looking at one element. “Not found” can only be said once everything has been checked.

wrong: In an else inside the loop
check.why: Only when every element has been compared can the method know the target is absent, so the “not found” answer comes after the loop's closing brace.

outro: “Search, count, total, smallest, average, a switch, and the fast search to finish. Each is a pattern from this hall, written as a method.”

question: Return the index of the first place target appears in the array, or -1 if it is not there.
signature: public int indexOf(int[] nums, int target)
hint: Return i from inside the loop the moment nums[i] matches. Return -1 after the loop.
feedback: Linear search as a method. Returning from inside the loop stops at the FIRST match, which is what makes the answer 0 for {4, 9, 4}. The -1 comes after the loop, because “not found” can only be said once every element has been checked.

question: Return how many times the target name appears in the array. Names match only when they are exactly the same, capital letters included.
signature: public int countName(String[] names, String target)
hint: Start a counter at 0 and add 1 each time names[i].equals(target). Do not stop at the first match.
feedback: A count accumulator: start at 0 before the loop, add 1 for each match, return after the loop. There is no break here — the job is to count every match, not to stop at the first. Strings are compared with .equals().

question: A list of expenses contains some negative numbers, which are errors. Return the total of the entries, ignoring any that are negative.
hint: Keep a total that starts at 0. Skip a negative entry with continue, or only add when the entry is 0 or more.
feedback: A sum accumulator with a filter in front of it. continue skips the rest of the pass for a negative entry and moves on to the next one. Writing if (entries[i] >= 0) around the addition does exactly the same job.

question: Return the smallest number in an array. The array will have at least one number, and the numbers may all be negative.
hint: Start min at nums[0], not at 0, and replace it whenever nums[i] is smaller.
feedback: A minimum starts from a real element — the first — and is replaced whenever something smaller turns up. Starting at 0 instead gives 0 for {12, 7, 9}, a number that is not even in the array. The loop can begin at index 1, since index 0 is already the starting value.

question: Return the average of the ratings in an array, keeping the decimal part: the average of 9, 7, 10, 8 and 7 is 8.2. The array will have at least one rating.
hint: Total the ratings in a loop, then divide — but cast the sum to double first, or the fraction is lost.
feedback: An average is a sum accumulator and one division. sum / ratings.length divides an int by an int and drops the fraction: 41 / 5 is 8. Casting one side first — (double) sum — makes it a double division and keeps the .2.

question: Return the description for a star rating: 5 is "Outstanding", 4 is "Good", 3 is "Satisfactory", 2 is "Poor" and 1 is "Terrible". Any other number is "Invalid".
hint: A switch on stars, with a return in each case and a default for everything else.
feedback: One value choosing between fixed answers is what a switch is for. Each case returns, and a return leaves the whole method, so no break is needed after it. default covers every other number — and it is what satisfies Java that the method always returns something.

question: The array is sorted from smallest to largest. Return the index where target is found, or -1 if it is not in the array.
signature: public int binarySearch(int[] sorted, int target)
hint: Keep low and high. While low <= high, look at the middle: return it on a match, otherwise move high to mid - 1 or low to mid + 1.
feedback: low and high fence in where the target could still be, and each pass looks only at the middle. Too big, and high moves to mid - 1; too small, and low moves to mid + 1. The - 1 and + 1 matter: without them the range can stop shrinking and the loop never ends. When low passes high the range is empty, and the answer is -1.
